body_text: Approval workflow software replaces manual approval methods with structured, automated processes that route requests, enforce rules, and log every decision. If your team still runs approvals through email threads, chat messages, or shared spreadsheets, this page will help you evaluate whether a purpose-built approval workflow solution fits your stack and your operations. Key Takeaways Modern approval workflow software automates request intake, conditional routing, notifications, and audit trails while running directly on existing data sources-databases, APIs, and SaaS tools-without forcing a data migration. Jet Admin lets teams build secure, custom approval workflows on top of their current stack, combining workflow automation, role-based permissions, and connected data in a single interface. Measurable outcomes from end-to-end approval workflows include reduced cycle time, improved SLA adherence, fewer errors from minimizing human mistakes, and stronger compliance reporting. Approval workflow software reduces approval turnaround time significantly and generates detailed audit trails for every decision, so leaders always know where a request stands. What is approval workflow software? Approval workflow software is a category of tools designed to orchestrate how requests, documents, transactions, or changes get formally reviewed and authorized before moving forward. Common use cases include invoice approvals, purchase orders, and employee onboarding, but the pattern extends to refund approvals, data-access requests, contract sign-offs, and more. At its core, the software replaces a manual process-someone emailing a PDF, pinging a manager in Slack, or updating a shared spreadsheet-with a structured approval process. Each approval request has a clear status (pending, approved, rejected), assigned approvers, and rules that determine routing. The software automatically sends alerts when action is needed, and it enables managers to view where requests are in the approval process at any moment. It is worth distinguishing approval workflow tools from generic workflow management or project management platforms. While task trackers handle timelines and collaboration, specialized approval software focuses on document approval workflows, role-based decisioning, audit trails, and rejection or rework loops. Core concepts you will see throughout this page include: the approval request (the submitted item), approver (the decision-maker), approval steps (the sequence), conditions (logic that determines paths), escalation (fallback when deadlines pass), the audit trail (timestamped log of all actions), and the approved asset (the final locked state after sign-off). Approval workflows appear across finance, HR, IT, legal, and operations. The principles are industry-agnostic: any process where someone must formally approve requests before work proceeds benefits from structured approval management. The operational problem: manual approvals and siloed data Picture a mid-size company in 2026. Invoices arrive and a finance analyst emails the PDF to a manager. Meanwhile, vacation requests live in a Google Sheet, and product change requests float through Slack threads. Each request lacks context-the invoice does not show the linked purchase order, the leave form is missing the manager's notes, and nobody knows who is responsible at each step. This is the norm for teams still running a manual approval process, and the costs are real. Manual approval processes often lead to lost or forgotten requests. Approval workflows can stall due to slow stakeholder responses. Version confusion increases the risk of human error in approvals, and scattered feedback across tools creates unnecessary manual work and rework. The business risks compound: late payments that forfeit vendor discounts, policy violations when spend exceeds authority, incorrect discounts or refunds slipping through, and unauthorized data access that creates compliance exposure. Without a single audit trail, reconstructing who approved what and when becomes a forensic exercise. Data fragmentation sits at the center of the problem. The information an approver needs-budget balances, customer history, vendor terms, prior decisions-lives in CRM, ERP, help-desk software, file storage, or data warehouses. Approvers toggle between apps, copy-paste data, and make decisions on incomplete information. The measurable impact: long cycle times, missed SLAs, low first-pass approval rates, high rework rates, and frustrated requesters. Over 60% of professionals report increased productivity with digital workflows, and 51% of professionals feel more productive with digital approval workflows-yet many organizations still rely on email and spreadsheets for critical decisions. Who approval workflow software is for Operations leaders care about consistency, SLA adherence, and throughput. They view approval process software as a lever to standardize how the organization handles procurement, refunds, vendor onboarding, and operational approvals. Their goal is to remove bottlenecks so internal teams can focus on work that moves the business forward, rather than chasing signatures. Product and growth teams deal with project approvals, experiment sign-offs, marketing spend, and creative asset reviews. Marketing teams need fast turnaround on campaign budgets and design proofs. These groups act as both requesters and approvers, and they want speed and clarity without sacrificing control. IT and data teams own access and change approvals, data security policies, and compliance enforcement. They need audit trails, granular permissions, and secure interfaces. They are also the ones integrating business systems and worrying about data integrity. Developers and internal tool builders configure the workflows themselves-authoring approval forms, designing roles and permissions, connecting data sources, and building automations. Approval workflow software enables teams to focus on strategic initiatives rather than administrative tasks, freeing engineering time for higher-value work. Cross-functional approvals span multiple groups. New vendor onboarding, for example, requires legal review, finance sign-off, and operations coordination. The software must support these multi-department processes with multiple stakeholders interacting as requesters, approvers, or administrators depending on context. Core capabilities of approval workflow software Any robust approval workflow tool should directly address the problems described above: delays, missing context, inconsistent processes, no audit trail, and poor visibility. Approval workflow software improves efficiency, consistency, and visibility across business functions, and it improves accountability with clear ownership of tasks at every step. Request intake forms let requesters submit structured information and attach related records-vendors, invoices, budget lines, tickets. Good forms validate inputs, enforce required fields, and pull context from upstream systems so nobody has to re-enter data. Centralized access to documents is essential for approval workflows, ensuring approvers have everything they need. Conditional routing uses a rules engine where rules determine which approver or group handles a request based on department, amount thresholds, requester role, or data sensitivity. Conditional approvals route low-risk items to a single approver while high-value business requests go through multiple levels. Multi-level approval hierarchies support both serial and parallel approval paths. Serial approvals move sequentially; parallel approvals go to multiple stakeholders simultaneously. Customizable approval flows enhance workflow efficiency by matching the actual decision structure of the organization. Notifications and reminders keep things moving. The software should include automated notifications for new assignments, pending approvals, and SLA breaches. Automated status changes streamline the approval process without manual intervention. Audit trails are crucial for tracking approval decisions. Every submission, approval, rejection, comment, and field change gets logged with timestamps and user identity. Reporting and dashboards surface key performance indicators like cycle time, SLA compliance, and bottleneck identification. Standardized workflows reduce incomplete submissions and inconsistent decision-making, and the data proves it. Permissions and security enforce role-based access, segregation of duties, and data visibility controls. The software allows organizations to define approval rules uniformly across departments. Modern approval management software automates routing and review processes, supports document approvals with version tracking and a final approved asset state, and handles exception paths like auto-approval under certain thresholds. With Jet Admin, teams can generate user interfaces for approval apps: dashboards that surface pending approvals, request forms that pull context from connected data, and detail views that show related records. The platform handles application logic, so you are not hand-coding every screen, permission check, or notification. An operations team might build a vendor onboarding flow that touches legal, procurement, and finance. It tracks the status of requests to identify bottlenecks, giving leaders the visibility they need to manage business operations effectively. Data model: approvals on top of your existing systems The data model matters because every approval process needs structured data-request records, related business objects, decisions, timestamps-tied back to source systems. Without this structure, you end up with the same fragmented mess that manual processes create. A typical approval data model includes these entities: the approval request record (the primary object), the requester (user or system that submitted), the approver or approvers (people or roles responsible for decisions), the related business object (invoice, order, ticket, dataset, or document), approval steps (the sequence with assigned roles and thresholds), decisions (approved, rejected, in rework), comments and justification, and audit log entries recording every action and field-level change. Jet Admin can map these entities onto existing tables and APIs rather than imposing a separate schema. For example, an approval request table can link to rows in a PostgreSQL invoice table via foreign key, or reference a CRM deal object by its source system ID. This means the document workflow stays connected to the system of record. If needed, Jet Admin-specific tables can store workflow metadata-status, assigned approver, SLA deadlines, escalation history-while still referencing IDs from upstream systems. This keeps the approval management system lightweight and avoids duplicating business data. The payoff: approvers see up-to-date information pulled live from source systems. When an approval happens, Jet Admin can write back to those systems or trigger external API calls-marking an invoice as approved for payment in the ERP, updating a CRM record, or notifying a downstream team. Business users interact with the same document or record they already trust, and the approval layer adds structure without replacing their existing systems. Screens and roles in a typical approval workflow app Clear screens and well-defined roles are critical for adoption. Requesters need simple approval forms. Approvers need focused dashboards. Admins need configuration views. If any of these experiences is clunky, people revert to email. Key screen types in an approval workflow app include: submission forms where requesters enter details and attach related data; inbox or queue views where approvers see their pending approvals filtered by status, SLA, and department; detailed request views showing the business object, history, related records, and a decision panel; history and audit views for compliance officers and leadership; and admin configuration screens where workflow rules, approval steps, and permissions are managed. Core roles map to how people interact with the system. The requester creates an approval request-an employee submitting an expense, a vendor submitting an invoice, a developer requesting access. The approver reviews and makes a decision: approve, reject, or send back for changes. The admin configures workflows, routing rules, and permissions. Observer or reporting roles give operations leads, compliance officers, or leadership read-only access to dashboards and audit trails. Jet Admin can provide different views per role. A finance approver dashboard might show only invoices above a certain threshold, with columns for vendor, amount, PO number, and due date. An operations admin screen might surface routing rules that can be modified without touching the underlying automation. A read-only audit screen might display the complete decision history for auditors reviewing financial documents. Designing approval workflows and automations Approval workflows in Jet Admin are modeled using automations driven by triggers, conditions, and actions. This approach lets teams design automated workflows that match their actual business processes rather than conforming to a rigid template. Triggers relevant to approvals include: a new record created or updated in a connected data source (such as a new invoice row in PostgreSQL), a webhook event from an external system, or scheduled jobs that run every minute, hour, or day to check for pending approvals or SLA breaches. These triggers initiate the workflow approval process automatically. Conditions determine routing. Amount thresholds, department, requester role, data sensitivity, document type, or custom fields can all branch the workflow. For example, purchase approvals under a set dollar amount might route to a single manager, while those above the threshold require a second approver from finance. These condition-based paths make the approval process software flexible enough to handle everything from employee requests to purchase orders. Actions execute the workflow: assigning the approval to a specific user or role, updating the request status, sending email or in-app notifications, calling external APIs to update an ERP or CRM, and writing audit-log entries. Automated reminders in approval workflow software help to prevent bottlenecks by nudging approvers when deadlines approach. Automated workflows eliminate email-based approval bottlenecks entirely. Multi-step approval processes can be serial (one approver after another), parallel (simultaneous review), or a mix. Rework cycles send rejected requests back to the requester with comments. Escalation rules trigger when deadlines pass-reassigning to a backup approver or notifying a manager. This kind of process automation handles repetitive tasks at scale while keeping the right people in the loop. End-to-end example: invoice approval workflow on Jet Admin Consider a company with 200 employees that processes several hundred vendor invoices per month. Before automation, the finance team received invoices via email, manually checked them against purchase orders in their ERP, then forwarded them to the appropriate manager for sign-off. The whole cycle took three to five days on average, and late payments were common. With Jet Admin, the invoice approval workflow starts when a new invoice record appears in the company's PostgreSQL database-either entered through an internal form or synced from a vendor portal. A Jet Admin automation detects the new record, creates an approval request, and auto-assigns it based on department and amount. Invoices under $5,000 go to the department manager. Those above $5,000 add a finance director as a second approver-a parallel approval path that runs simultaneously with the manager review. The approver opens their dashboard and sees the invoice alongside key fields pulled live from the database: vendor name, amount, PO reference, due date, and any policy flags. Related data from the CRM or ERP-vendor payment history, outstanding balance, contract terms-is surfaced in the same view. No app-switching, no copy-paste. The approver can approve, reject with comments, or request changes. If a request sits pending for more than 48 hours, an automated reminder fires. After 72 hours, the workflow escalates to the finance director regardless of amount. Approval software centralizes requests and tracks decisions in real-time, so leadership always knows the status of every invoice. When the final approval lands, the automation writes back to the source database, marking the invoice as approved for payment. The complete audit trail-who submitted, who approved, timestamps, comments, any rework-is logged and available for reporting. Dashboards show cycle time, SLA compliance, and volume trends. The approval workflow reduces errors by minimizing human mistakes that plagued the old email-based process, and the finance team now closes the same document approval in under 24 hours on average. Security, permissions, and audit trails Security matters most when approval workflows handle spend, customer data, HR records, or access rights. For operations, IT, and organizations facing regulatory requirements, weak controls are not an option. Role-based permissions control who can create, view, edit, approve, or administer workflows. An approval workflow tool should ensure approvers only see the data they need-a manager reviewing team approvals should not see salary data for other departments. Jet Admin can leverage access controls tied to both data sources and app-level permissions, restricting sensitive information like salaries, discount rates, or PII to appropriate roles. Jet Admin supports external authentication providers including Auth0, Google OAuth, and OIDC, so identity management stays centralized. A strong audit trail captures who submitted, who approved each step, timestamps of every action, decisions and rejections, comments, field changes, and integration calls. This is not just a compliance checkbox-it is the foundation for incident reviews, process improvement, and data security audits. Approval workflow software maintains compliance through consistent documentation processes. Specialized software improves compliance and audit readiness by making every decision traceable. Segregation of duties is critical for high-value approvals. The same person should not create and approve their own invoice or expense. Approval tools can enforce this technically-blocking self-approval, requiring a different role for the second step, or flagging violations. Centralized approval processes reduce misunderstandings and lost feedback because every decision, comment, and revision lives in one system with clear ownership. Integrations: running approvals on your existing stack Integrations are the foundation of effective workflow approval software. Without them, approval tools become isolated silos that duplicate data and create more problems than they solve. Jet Admin connects to common categories of tools: relational databases (PostgreSQL, MySQL), data warehouses (BigQuery, Snowflake), file and object storage (Amazon S3, Google Cloud Storage), CRMs (HubSpot, Salesforce), support systems (Zendesk), communication tools (Slack, Gmail, SendGrid), and authentication providers (Auth0, Google OAuth). When a discount is approved, the CRM record updates automatically. When a refund request completes, a notification posts to a Slack channel. When an access request is granted, the system triggers a provisioning API. Data integration means approvals run on live business data, not stale exports. Because Jet Admin runs on top of existing data, teams avoid large data migrations and keep their existing workflows and systems of record intact. IT and developers can standardize APIs and data models behind Jet Admin so new approval processes reuse existing integration work. This is especially valuable for organizations scaling from one approval workflow to many. Automated workflows allow quick remote approvals via mobile devices, and the software offers mobile access for approvals away from desks-meaning approvers are not blocked just because they are traveling or working remotely. Build vs. buy: packaged tools vs. Jet Admin The "build vs. buy" decision is one of the first questions teams face when evaluating the best approval workflow software. The options are: buy a packaged approval tool, build a fully custom internal app, or use a platform like Jet Admin that sits between the two. Packaged approval tools offer faster initial setup for narrow use cases. Many approval tools in the market serve specific niches well-Wrike is used by 20,000 organizations worldwide for project and workflow management; Filestage simplifies content review for agencies and marketing teams; DocuWare automates document approvals with a clear audit trail; Moxo is designed for external approval workflows across teams. However, these point solutions often force data migration, limit UI customization, and struggle when your internal workflows diverge from their templates. Tools like Microsoft Power Automate or Power Automate-based solutions can handle some approval scenarios, but may require significant configuration for complex multi-system flows. Approval Studio is another option focused on creative review. The tradeoff: faster start, less flexibility over time. But the cost is high: longer build cycles, dedicated engineering resources, technical debt, and ongoing maintenance for auth, UI scaffolding, data connectors, and audit logging. What are your compliance and data security requirements? How fast do you need to iterate? What internal engineering capacity do you have? If the answers point toward multiple workflows, deep integration needs, and limited engineering bandwidth, a platform approach makes strong economic sense. Implementation path: from first workflow to organization-wide approvals Teams adopting Jet Admin for approval workflows typically follow a phased approach, starting small and expanding as confidence and reuse grow. In the first phase, identify one or two high-friction processes-invoice approvals or refund approvals are common starting points. Even a simple workflow at this stage demonstrates value and surfaces real feedback. The second phase incorporates that feedback. Refine request forms based on what approvers actually need to see. Adjust routing thresholds-maybe the initial cutoff was too low, or too many requests hit the escalation path. Introduce basic reporting dashboards to monitor cycle times, bottlenecks, and SLA miss rates. This is where existing workflows start to feel materially better. In the third phase, expand to adjacent workflows: purchase approvals, access requests, expense approvals, document creation sign-offs, or vendor onboarding. Standardize roles and permissions across workflows, and reuse components-shared lookup tables, common notification templates, and integration connectors already configured. Automated approval workflows save teams hundreds of hours annually as the number of automated processes grows. The fourth phase is governance. Document workflows. Train admins on rule changes. Establish change management practices-test rule updates in a non-production environment before deploying. Set up periodic reviews of metrics to continuously improve standardized approval processes. Approval workflow systems can scale with an organization's growth without compromising efficiency, but only if governance keeps pace with adoption. Reporting and continuous improvement of approval processes Reporting is not a nice-to-have. Leaders and operations teams need to see how approval processes perform and where to optimize, not just that the workflows exist. Without measurement, you cannot justify continued investment or identify where business processes are breaking down. Key metrics to track and visualize include: cycle time from submission to final approval, on-time SLA rate, first-pass approval rate (how often requests are approved without rework), rework or rejection rate, volume by department or approver, and queue length or backlog. Approval workflow software reduces approval turnaround time significantly when teams actively monitor and act on these numbers. An approval workflow tool like Jet Admin can use connected data to build dashboards that combine approval metrics with business outcomes. For example: total spend by approved invoices, refund amounts correlated with churn risk, or access requests mapped against security incidents. This turns the approval tracking system into a decision-support tool for leadership. Teams should use this data to refine rules over time: adjusting thresholds, adding or removing approval steps, rebalancing workloads across approvers, and automating more low-risk decisions. If the data shows that 95% of requests under a certain amount are approved without changes, that is a candidate for automated approval. If one approver consistently has a backlog, redistribute or escalate earlier. FAQ: evaluating and running approval workflow software This section answers common questions operations, IT, and product teams have about approval workflow tools and Jet Admin specifically. Each answer adds detail not fully covered above. How is approval workflow software different from generic project management tools? Approval software focuses on structured approval processes with clear states (pending, approved, rejected), conditional routing based on rules, formal audit trails, and rejection or rework loops. Project management tools primarily track tasks, timelines, and collaboration. Many teams pair both: project management for planning and execution, approval management software for formal sign-offs that gate critical actions like finance approvals, team approvals, or document approval processes. The key difference is that approval tools enforce decisions and accountability, not just progress. Can we start with one approval process and expand later? Yes, and this is the most common pattern. Teams typically pilot with a single workflow-such as an invoice approval workflow or access request approvals-validate the data model, roles, and routing logic, and then reuse those patterns to add more business requests over time. Because integrations and permissions are configured once and reused, each subsequent workflow builds faster. You do not need to re-implement data connectors or authentication for every new process. How does Jet Admin handle changes to approval rules over time? Admins can adjust routing rules, conditions, thresholds, and automations without rewriting the entire app. For example, if a new spending policy changes the threshold for second-level approval, an admin updates the condition in the workflow builder. Using versioning practices and testing in a non-production environment helps avoid disruption. This flexibility matters because approval rules change as organizations grow and policies evolve. What happens if one of our integrated systems is temporarily unavailable? Robust approval workflow tools should surface error states clearly in the UI rather than silently failing. Strategies include queueing actions to retry when the system recovers, designing workflows that degrade gracefully (for example, allowing the approval to proceed while flagging the failed write-back), and coordinating with IT/DevOps on monitoring and incident response. No system is immune to outages, but a well-designed workflow minimizes the blast radius. How long does it typically take to implement a basic approval workflow in Jet Admin? For a well-scoped workflow with existing integrations and clear business rules, teams typically go from design to deployment in days to a couple of weeks. More complex workflows-those involving multiple source systems, intricate branching logic, or strict compliance requirements-may take several weeks. Actual timelines depend on data readiness, stakeholder availability, and whether document creation and routing rules are already well understood. Starting with a focused pilot is the best way to establish a realistic baseline. If your team is ready to move beyond email-based approvals, explore how Jet Admin's automations and integrations can help you build secure approval workflows on your existing data-without a forced migration or months of custom engineering.

body_text: If you’re planning a construction project in Schenectady, New York , your first step is understanding how the city handles building permits. Schenectady’s permitting process is managed at the city level, with its own requirements for building, electrical, plumbing, and inspections. This guide walks through what requires a permit, how to submit a Schenectady building permit application, what fees to expect, and how the approval and inspection process works from start to finish. Whether you’re managing a commercial project or residential build, this will help you move through Schenectady permitting with fewer delays and fewer surprises. Simplify permitting in Schenectady with PermitFlow. Learn how. ‍ What requires a building permit in Schenectady? In the City of Schenectady, most construction, repair, and alteration work requires a permit. The city applies this requirement broadly, so even smaller projects can trigger permitting depending on the scope. Projects that typically require a building permit include: New construction Additions and enlargements Alterations and improvements Moving or relocating a structure Demolition Installation of a solid-fuel-burning heating appliance, chimney, or flue in a dwelling unit Repairs that affect structure, egress, building systems, or fire protection ‍ What doesn’t require a building permit? Schenectady’s code lists these exemptions: One-story detached tool sheds, storage sheds, playhouses, and similar structures associated with 1- and 2-family homes or townhouses, if they are 144 sq. ft. or less Swings and other playground equipment for 1- and 2-family homes or townhouses Above-ground swimming pools for 1- and 2-family homes or townhouses if designed for a water depth of less than 24 inches Fences that are not part of a pool enclosure Retaining walls, unless they support a surcharge or impound Class I, II, or IIIA liquids Temporary motion-picture, television, and theater stage sets and scenery Window awnings supported by an exterior wall of a 1- or 2-family home or townhouse Partitions or movable cases under 5 feet 9 inches high Painting, wallpapering, tiling, carpeting, and similar finish work Installation of listed portable electrical, plumbing, heating, ventilation, cooling equipment, or appliances ‍ Schenectady building permit fees The City of Schenectady charges building permit fees based on project value and whether the work is residential or commercial. See how. ‍ How to get a building permit in Schenectady Building permits in the City of Schenectady are issued by the City Building Department . Residential and commercial construction projects must follow the city’s application, review, and inspection process, which is administered locally and enforced under the New York State Uniform Fire Prevention and Building Code and Energy Code. ‍ Step 1: Prepare your plans and documents The City of Schenectady requires a complete submittal before plan review begins. Incomplete applications can delay review or result in rejection. Typical submittal requirements include: Detailed scope of work: A written description of the proposed construction, including materials, dimensions, and structural changes Construction cost estimate: Used to calculate permit fees Stamped plans (when required): Projects involving structural work or requiring design professionals must be prepared and stamped by a New York State Licensed Architect or Professional Engineer Workers’ compensation documentation: Submit Form C-105.2, U-26.3, or CE-200 exemption form, as applicable Contractor information: Trade work such as electrical or plumbing must be performed by properly licensed contractors where required by city regulations ‍ Step 2: Submit your application The City of Schenectady accepts building permit applications through its permitting system and by mail or fax (518-372-9459) to the Building Inspector’s Office. The permit must be posted in a visible location at the job site for the duration of construction. ‍ Step 5: Begin work and schedule inspections Inspections are required throughout construction to verify compliance and close out the permit. title: It turns out people like speaking to an AI moderator
summary: Are people willing to talk to an AI interviewer? Motives shares real participant reactions — and why video-based AI interviews unlock more honest answers.
body_text: At Motives, we often hear one question: "Are people actually willing to talk to an AI interviewer?" Especially when it comes to video interviews, there's understandable skepticism about whether anyone would feel comfortable having a heart-to-heart with artificial intelligence. We’ve taken this really seriously since the beginning - in classic lean startup fashion, our MVP was our CTO Sam pretending to be an AI: we told participants to join a Zoom call and that they’d be interviewed by an AI in the chat, while Sam (with his camera off) copy/pasted their responses from the transcription into ChatGPT, and then copy/pasted those back. Despite the obvious limitations of this first version, participants already seemed comfortable enough for us to proceed with more development From those humble beginnings, we’ve built a fully featured AI moderator for video calls: it speaks out loud and has a natural-feeling conversation with participants, who are themselves speaking out loud the whole time just like they’re joining a regular video call. And their reactions have surprised even us. Not only are people willing to talk to our AI interviewer - they genuinely enjoy it. Recent feedback from participants tells the story: "It felt like speaking to a real person. I was impressed by the responses and how naturally the conversation flowed." "The interview was much better than I anticipated. The questions and follow-up actually aligned with what I was saying." "It was very relaxing, and I felt free to say whatever without having anybody judge me." The power of a judgment-free zone That last point highlights something fascinating about AI interviewers: they create a unique, neutral space where people feel safe being completely honest. We’ve found that people have consistently reported being more honest in our AI-moderated interviews than they might be with a human moderator. This effect shows up consistently across various sensitive topics: Private health discussions Personal finance conversations Brutally honest product feedback General personal matters On reflection, this makes sense - the AI can create a neutral space where participants can feel more comfortable expressing their true thoughts and feelings. There's no need to worry about impressing the interviewer or managing their reactions. It also takes away worries about mismatches between the backgrounds of the interviewees and the moderators - for example, imagine a young person interviewing seniors about their personal finance struggles. An AI moderator creates a space where participants feel acknowledged, without the shadow of human subjectivity or bias. The difference real conversation makes Not all AI interviews are created equal. Motives conducts real video conversations where people can speak naturally, just as they would with a human interviewer. Most other “AI researchers” rely on (or primarily utilize) text-based chat. This difference matters. As one recent participant explained: "I've taken other interviews before with AI. But those felt computerized and difficult to understand - just typing back and forth. This was different. When I'm talking here, it really feels like I'm talking with a real person because everything feels so humanized. The voice, the responses, the natural flow of conversation... I really need this kind of interaction." Many people claim they've tested AI researcher and found that they "don't work." Almost always, they're referring to to text-based moderators. Seeing a video-call-based AI moderator changes everything: the ability to speak naturally, hear a warm, responsive voice, and engage in authentic dialogue creates a a transformative experience. A real spoken conversation lets people to focus on their thoughts rather than their writing, encouraging open an authentic self-expression that leads to richer insights. One question we often get: No, the AI isn’t a creepy, overly lifelike 3D rendering of a fake human. It’s simply a minimal avatar that smiles and blinks as it speaks. In our testing, this strikes the perfect balance—human enough to make the conversation feel natural, but far from the discomfort of the uncanny valley. Why this matters for research Getting genuinely honest feedback is one of the biggest challenges in qualitative research. Social dynamics, politeness, and the desire to avoid conflict can all get in the way of uncovering real insights. AI interviewers offer a solution to this challenge. By creating a space where people feel comfortable being completely candid, we can gather deeper, more authentic insights about everything from product concepts to personal experiences. And with the quality of the interviews being so good, you can then take advantage of all of the other benefits of AI-led qualitative research: rapid speed and much larger scale. It's not just a more effective way to conduct research - it's also a more pleasant experience for everyone involved. ‍ Interested in seeing how AI interviews could help you gather more authentic insights? Let's talk about how Motives can support your research goals.

title: TLX591-Tx ProstACT SELECT Study Published in Cancers Journal
summary: Our mission is to help patients with cancer live longer with better quality lives
body_text: TLX591-Tx ProstACT SELECT Study Published in Cancers Journal Melbourne (Australia) and Indianapolis, IN (United States) | July 22, 2026 Peer-reviewed publication of ProstACT SELECT [1] results confirm the utility of 68Ga (gallium)-PSMA-PET imaging to select patients for TLX591-Tx therapy using a theranostic approach [2] . Consistent with previously reported results [3] , the publication highlights TLX591-Tx’s clinical differentiation and safety profile. TLX591-Tx, Telix’s lead PSMA-targeting rADC therapy candidate, is currently being evaluated in ProstACT Global Phase 3 study [4] for advanced metastatic prostate cancer. Telix today announced publication of results from the ProstACT SELECT study in Cancers , a peer-reviewed journal. The Phase 1 study evaluated TLX591-Tx (lutetium-177 (177Lu) rosopatamab tetraxetan), Telix’s first-in-class prostate-specific membrane antigen (PSMA) targeting radio antibody-drug conjugate (rADC) therapy candidate. The study’s scientific purpose was to evaluate lesion concordance between 68Ga-PSMA-PET [5] and multi-time point SPECT [6] imaging for patient selection using a “theranostic” approach. The publication highlights TLX591-Tx’s differentiated clinical profile, including an intensified dosing schedule, prolonged tumor retention and low exocrine (salivary) gland irradiation. The authors also concluded that in a heterogeneous population representative of a real-world setting, TLX591-Tx therapy in combination with standard of care (SOC) demonstrated a manageable and predictable safety profile, and indicative efficacy with a median radiographic progression-free survival (rPFS) of 8.8 months reported in evaluable patients. Nat Lenzo, MD, Nuclear Medicine Oncologist and Principal Investigator on the ProstACT SELECT study commented, “A key objective of ProstACT SELECT was to determine whether PSMA-PET imaging could reliably identify patients suitable for TLX591-Tx therapy, and the results clearly support this approach. The results provide compelling evidence that the PSMA-PET imaging agent and TLX591-Tx are targeting the same disease sites, supporting the ongoing ProstACT Global trial for mCRPC [7] , where there remains significant unmet need for additional treatment options.” David N. Cade, MD, Group Chief Medical Officer, Telix, said, “The publication of ProstACT SELECT data further strengthens the scientific foundation for Telix’s lead therapeutic candidate, TLX591-Tx. The peer-reviewed results support our patient-selection strategy and demonstrate a differentiated pharmacologic profile characterized by durable tumor targeting, hepatobiliary clearance, and a manageable safety profile. Telix is further evaluating TLX591-Tx in the international multi-center Phase 3 ProstACT Global study, where we aim to meaningfully improve outcomes for patients living with advanced prostate cancer.” The full paper is available at: https://www.mdpi.com/3989748 About ProstACT SELECT The purpose of the ProstACT SELECT trial was to evaluate the utility of 68Ga-PSMA-PET imaging (Illuccix) to select patients for TLX591-Tx rADC therapy. The primary objectives were to determine whole body biodistribution and organ radiation dosimetry and assess the safety and tolerability of TLX591-Tx in patients with advanced mCRPC. rPFS was a secondary study objective. TLX591-Tx has not received a marketing authorization in any jurisdiction [1] ClinicalTrials.gov ID: NCT04786847 . [2] Lenzo et al. Cancers. 2026. [3] Telix ASX disclosures October 19, 2023 and May 31, 2024. [4] ClinicalTrials.gov ID: NCT06520345 . [5] Imaging of prostate-specific membrane antigen with positron emission tomography. [6] Single-photon emission computed tomography. [7] Metastatic castration-resistant prostate cancer.

title: How to Keep Your Backpack Clean (and Looking New All Year)
summary: Backpacks go through a lot in a school year. They sit on classroom floors, ride in cars and buses, carry water bottles, hold half-finished snacks, and somehow collect crumbs in pockets you barely use. The good news: keeping a backpack clean does not have to be complicated. With a few simple habits, regular spot checks, and the right care routine, you can help your backpack stay fresh from the first day of school through the last. And when you start with a washable, well-organized Vera Bradley backpack, everyday messes are much easier to manage. Start With a Weekly Backpack Cleanout The easiest way to keep a backpack clean is to stop little messes from becoming bigger ones. Once a week, empty every compartment and shake out crumbs, scraps of paper, pencil shavings, receipts, wrappers, and anything else that has settled at the bottom. Shop the Large Bancroft Backpack Check smaller pockets, too. Pens, lip balm, snacks, sticky notes, and loose change are easy to forget, but they are often the source of stains, smells, and clutter. 💡 Pro Tip: It can be hard to keep track of all the little things you might need every day. Try a small pouch or two to hold those extras in your backpack. Having them all zipped in one place makes them easy to find, plus it’s a breeze to pull out the pouch when it’s cleanout time. Keep Food and Drinks Contained Snacks and water bottles are usually the biggest backpack mess-makers. Use a lunch bag or reusable container instead of dropping food directly into a backpack pocket. For water bottles, use exterior side pockets whenever possible so leaks are less likely to spread to books, papers, or your laptop. This is where backpack design matters. Styles with side bottle pockets, zip compartments, and interior organization make it easier to separate school supplies, snacks, tech, and personal items. 💡 Pro Tip: Hydration is great. A loose water bottle rolling around inside your bag? Not so much. Look for a backpack like Vera Bradley’s Large Bancroft Backpack which has a side pocket with elastic and a pleat to fit a variety of different-sized bottles. Store Pens, Pencils, and Small Supplies An uncapped pen can do a lot of damage in a backpack. Keep writing tools in a pencil pouch or dedicated pocket instead of loose in the main compartment. Choose a backpack that has pen slips, zip pockets, and interior compartments to keep smaller supplies from rolling around. Bonus: you know exactly where your pen is when you need it! Shop Vera Bradley Backpacks Choose Easy-to-Clean Materials Some backpack messes are unavoidable but the right material can make cleanup a lot easier. When you’re shopping for a school backpack, look for fabrics that are designed to handle everyday use and are easy to clean when life gets messy. And always follow the manufacturer’s recommended cleaning instructions when it comes time for a refresh. Vera Bradley’s backpacks not only look great, they are a durable, practical pick. In fact, our quilted Premium Cotton backpacks can actually be tossed in the washing machine to take off that mid-school year grime. Follow these steps to keep your backpack looking like new: How to Clean a Vera Bradley Backpack 1. Before washing your quilted cotton Vera Bradley backpack, empty it completely. Check every pocket, remove loose items, and shake out crumbs or debris. 2. Close all zippers and closures before placing the bag in the washing machine. 3. Wash in cold water on a gentle cycle with mild detergent. 4. Line dry or lay your backpack flat to dry to help maintain its shape. Have a Featherweight backpack? Skip the washing machine – clean stains with a soft, damp cloth and gentle detergent, then rinse thoroughly and lay flat to dry. How Often Should You Clean Your Backpack? For backpacks that get everyday use, a little routine maintenance goes a long way. Do a quick cleanout once a week and spot clean any spills or stains that pop up. If your backpack is machine washable, do a more thorough wash cycle each semester to remove lingering odors and start fresh. Empty it, organize it, wipe what needs wiping, and wash when needed. That is the simplest way to keep your backpack looking newer for longer! A Great Day Starts With a Clean Backpack Your backpack carries your whole day. Choosing a washable, thoughtfully-designed backpack makes it easier to handle real-life messes without letting them take over. With regular cleanouts, smart packing habits, and the right care routine, your backpack can stay fresh, organized, and ready for whatever the school year brings! SHOP ALL SCHOOL BACKPACKS

title: Parman Energy Group: The 90-Year Path to Employee Ownership
summary: Parman Energy Group made MDM's 2025 Lubricants and Fuels list. Here's how a 1930s Nashville jobber became employee-owned and bought a tractor dealer.
body_text: Part of Distributor Playbooks — strategy teardowns of every company on the 2025 MDM Top Distributors lists . Parman Energy Group showed up on MDM's 2025 Top Distributors list in the Lubricants & Fuels vertical, one of the quieter names on a roster full of household ones. That is by design. Parman has spent nine decades building a Chevron lubricants and commercial fuel business out of Nashville, and somewhere along the way it made a decision most petroleum jobbers in a private-equity-hungry sector never make: it sold itself entirely to its own employees. A Nashville corner-store business, 1930s style Bates Parman started Parman Oil Company in downtown Nashville in the mid-1930s, selling petroleum products to local service stations. For nearly fifty years it stayed a regional fuel jobber, the kind of business that lives or dies on relationships with a handful of station owners and a fleet of delivery trucks. Nothing about its first half-century predicted where it would end up. The 1978 buyout that changed the trajectory The pivot came in 1978, when three partners, Don Crichton, Johnny Jewell, and Jimmy Jewell, bought the company from the Parman family. Their biggest move came in 1986: acquiring Southern Oil Company, a Quaker State, Castrol, and Chevron distributor, which forced a relocation to a larger West Nashville facility and effectively turned a single-brand fuel jobber into a multi-brand lubricants distributor. That acquisition set the template Parman still runs today: grow by buying adjacent petroleum businesses rather than by winning share brand by brand. Through the 1980s and 90s the company layered on a second business line almost by accident. It bought Williams Lubrication Equipment Sales & Service Company, a regional player in dispensing hardware since the mid-1950s, and folded it into a new Parman Lubricants Corporation. That equipment arm is now a real differentiator: the company markets itself as the largest stocking distributor of fuel, lubrication, and DEF storage tanks and dispensing equipment in its territory, and calls itself the market leader in diesel exhaust fluid distribution, according to its own site . Selling the tank and the pump alongside the fluid is a stickier sale than selling fluid alone, and it's the kind of unglamorous adjacency that rarely shows up in a distributor's marketing but shows up in its renewal rates. The rebrand nobody outside Nashville noticed By 2000 the company had become, in its own words, a fully integrated supplier of fuels, lubricants, and dispensing equipment, adding a Chattanooga facility that year and pushing further into West Tennessee. In June 2009 it rebranded from Parman Oil to Parman Energy, a name change that tracked the reality of the business better than the old one did. The company has since carried Chevron's 1st Source Elite Marketer designation in most years, a status Chevron reserves for distributors that go beyond moving product. The unusual bet: selling the company to its own workforce Here is the move that separates Parman from most of the vertical. In February 2015, Parman converted to full employee ownership through an ESOP. In 2018 it took the name Parman Energy Group and folded its holding structure around it. Fuel and lubricant distribution has spent the last decade consolidating into private-equity-backed platforms chasing scale and multiple expansion. Parman went the other direction, locking ownership inside the workforce that runs the trucks and the counters. CEO Rachel Hockenberger, who joined the company as a temp and rose to the top job over a 20-year run, has described the ESOP model as demanding, not automatic: it requires the company to actually behave like the workers own it, in how routes are run and how customers are treated, not just on paper. That ownership structure is the piece worth naming plainly: an ESOP-owned distributor competing in a sector where the dominant playbook is roll-up-and-flip is a genuinely different bet on how you retain route drivers and counter staff for decades, not quarters. Building sideways, not just bigger The M&A engine never stopped. In October 2023, Parman Holdings Corporation (the ESOP parent) acquired Brad Hall Fuel's commercial fuel business in Morristown, Tennessee, its 7th supply and distribution location , extending a footprint that now spans Tennessee, Mississippi, Arkansas, and a newer beachhead in Minnesota. President Robert Giffin framed it as raising the product line in the greater Knoxville market; Hockenberger framed it as growing brand value for the employee-owners who hold it. What's more telling is where the holding company chose to diversify. Rather than pour every dollar back into fuel and lubricant volume, Parman Holdings built out Parman Tractor & Equipment, an agricultural and construction equipment dealer arm, alongside a properties division. It's a sideways move: petroleum distribution and farm equipment retail share almost nothing operationally except rural customers and a service-truck mentality, but they share a customer base that trusts the same brand for diesel and dirt work. On Nashville Business Journal's 2025 fastest-growing companies list , Parman Holdings ranked 21st with $271.2 million in 2024 revenue and 190 employees, growth MDM's own Lubricants & Fuels entry for Parman Energy specifically doesn't itemize, since the company doesn't disclose divisional figures. The shape of the bet Parman's story reads less like a growth chart and more like a series of decisions to stay independent on its own terms: buy the adjacent petroleum business, then the equipment arm that locks in the relationship, then hand the whole thing to the people running it, then diversify into a completely different rural retail category rather than chase pure fuel-volume scale. None of those moves is dramatic on its own. Stacked across ninety years, they explain why a company most of the industry hasn't heard of just made a national ranking anyway. Distributors like Parman win or lose on decisions made decades before anyone outside the trade notices: which brand to carry, which small business to buy, who gets to own the result. The MDM Top Distributors list is a snapshot of that slow arithmetic, one branch and one acquisition at a time.

By connecting our purpose with our strategy, we put impact at the heart of how we innovate and help address some of the world's most pressing challenges." "The progress reflected in this report demonstrates what is possible when innovation, customer value and purpose work together to improve the health of animals and the lives of the people who depend on them." title: Addendum vs. Amendment: What's the Difference? | ROGER Blog
summary: Learn the difference between an addendum and an amendment in contracts. Discover when to use each, how they impact agreements, and tips for managing contract changes effectively.
body_text: ❓What is an amendment to a contract? An amendment modifies the existing content of a contract. Think of it as editing what’s already there. This could involve changing a date, adjusting payment terms, revising a scope of work, or even replacing a section altogether. Amendments are common when business needs shift or when both parties agree that certain terms no longer apply. Instead of drafting an entirely new contract, you simply amend the one you already have. 📌 Example: You originally agreed to deliver a project by June 1, but the client needs more time. An amendment could change the delivery deadline to July 15. An amendment must be agreed upon, and ideally signed, by all involved parties to be legally binding.. ❓What is an addendum to a contract? An addendum is like an attachment that adds new terms or information to a contract without changing the original wording. It complements the existing agreement rather than altering it. Addenda are used when you want to expand the contract's scope, insert additional responsibilities, or add clarifying details that weren’t included in the original document. 📌 Example: You sign a lease agreement, then decide to rent a parking space from the same landlord. Instead of rewriting the lease, a simple addendum can outline the new parking arrangement. An addendum should reference the original contract and be signed by all parties to ensure clarity and enforceability. ❓When should you use an amendment vs. an addendum? The key difference lies in what you're trying to change : Use an amendment when you're altering existing terms within a contract. Use an addendum when you're adding new terms or details to supplement the agreement. In other words, if the content in the original contract needs to be revised , go with an amendment. If you're adding extra provisions , opt for an addendum. When in doubt, consider whether the contract language needs to be edited or expanded. That can usually point you in the right direction. ❓Can you use both in the same agreement? Yes, and it happens more often than you'd think. A contract may go through several updates during its lifecycle. You might start with a standard agreement, later add new conditions via an addendum, and eventually amend the original terms based on changing circumstances. Just be sure each change is clearly labeled and documented so there’s no confusion. For ongoing relationships, like vendor contracts or service agreements. It’s common to issue multiple amendments and addenda over time. ❓Are amendments and addenda legally binding? Absolutely! A s long as they’re properly executed . To be enforceable: All parties must agree to the changes The language should be clear and specific The document should reference the original contract It’s best practice for all parties to sign the updated document Having both the original contract and its updates stored in a central location (like your contract management platform) makes compliance easier and audit trails stronger. ❓Do I need to draft a new contract instead? Not always. If the core structure of the contract remains intact and the changes are minimal or additive, an amendment or addendum will usually do the job. However, if you’re overhauling major portions of the agreement, or the business relationship has significantly changed. It might be smarter to draft a brand-new contract . Starting fresh can help reduce confusion and consolidate all obligations into one updated document. ❓What's the best way to manage addenda and amendments? T he best way? Keep it simple, consistent, and organised. If you're managing contracts manually, make sure to: Number your amendments/addenda clearly (e.g., “Addendum #2”) Reference the date and title of the original contract Ensure all parties sign the update Store updated documents alongside the original agreement Better yet, consider using contract management software like ROGER to streamline the process. With smart version control, document tracking, and built-in e-signatures , you can keep all your contracts, and their modification. Easy to access and audit. While both addenda and amendments allow you to update contracts, they play different roles. Amendments edit existing terms , while addenda add new information . Knowing when and how to use each helps keep your agreements accurate, up-to-date, and legally sound. 📝 Looking for more contract tips?
